newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan agrees to special treatment of HK passports.
newsitem.headline: Japan agrees to special treatment of HK passports.

text.p: Japan has agreed to treat passports of Hong Kong residents differently from Chinese passports after the territory's reversion to China in 1997, Hong Kong governor Chris Patten said on Thursday.

The agreement was reached in meetings between Patten and Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and separately with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Thursday, Patten told Reuters in an exclusive interview.
"I am grateful to them (Hashimoto and Ikeda) that they confirmed that holders of SAR (Special Administrative Region) passports will be treated differently from a Chinese passport," Patten said.
But Patten did not clarify what specific measures Japan was ready to afford Hong Kong's post-1997 passports.

Japan's Foreign Ministry officials told reporters earlier on Thursday that Tokyo is still considering how to treat passports to be issued by the Hong Kong SAR but intends to give them more favourable treatment than those of China.
Patten had been trying to persuade Japan to afford holders of Hong Kong's post-1997 passports visa-free entry similar to holders of British passports.
So far only Britain, Singapore and Western Samoa have promised SAR passport holders visa-free entry.
Patten said it was important for Hong Kong residents to be able to continue to freely visit Japan, which is an important trade partner for the British colony.
"It's important not only commercially, but in terms of self-confidence (of the Hong Kong people)," Patten said.
More than 150 years of British colonial rule will end at midnight next June 30 when Hong Kong reverts to China as a Special Administrative Region.
